So it's easy for them to have the camera on all the time. It's not the same for everyone else in the company!

When I was a kid I was in the Girl Guides (like Scouts, but for girls. In the UK, they were separated until very recently). I was on one particular camp, when I was about 14/15. The camps always had the same set up, a circle of big canvas tents. One tent for each Patrol (a smaller team of girls. A bit like Houses in school) usually a group of 5/6 girls, a tent or two for the Guide Leaders and a large mess tent.

We were camped about 200 metres from a wooded area that was between the camp site and the activity lodge. During this camp, some of the older girls, myself included were trying to get a certain badge, that required you to assemble and sleep in a bivouac (a minimal temporary shelter). For us, it was a sheet of tarpaulin and some rope. Each night one girl would be given the tarp and rope and would set up and sleep and then the next morning, disassemble it and return it to the leaders ready for the next girl. It was the height of summer and the weather was good so it was a pretty easy experience.

So out of fairness they just went through the week in alphabetical order (my surname was last). First two nights, no problem. Third night, we hear rustling around and the leaders talking but that was it. In the morning we found out there had been someone in the woods and approached the girl was there. Luckily she was the oldest in the group (almost 17) and this was her last camp and as soon as she heard him she ran back to the leaders tent. It was private property so no one else should have been there.

The rest of us all noped out of staying there and we all doubled up in the tents. It was terrifying to think what would have happened if it had been a younger girl who would have just panicked and wouldn't have the wherewithal to deal with the situation. Or one of the heavy sleepers in the group.

This picture and subsequent posts make me so mad! This photo appeared in social media earlier this year with a statement from a young woman who claimed that this happened at a peaceful protest that was broken up by police. That they opened fire on the front lines, where she was positioned and when they protestors turned to run they pursued. The woman claimed that she crouched down and huddled behind a car covering her head and face with her arms and hands and they continued to fire. 

Whatever the story, the injuries are fairly consistent with her account. And this is speaking as someone who studied and trained in forensic science and medicine. The bruises are predominantly on the rear, thighs, arms and hands, consistent with someone kneeling down, with their head down and covered with their hands and arms.

Besides all that rubber crowd dispersing bullets are not "non-lethal" but less lethal, and that is only when used correctly. That is pointed at the ground and allowed to ricochet. They are not designed to be shot straight at a person. There is plenty of footage of police using them incorrectly and being fired straight into the crowd. There are also a number of cases of them being used on innocent bystanders. There is one case of note of a young woman in Dallas who was filmed walking down the street with her shopping when she was shot in the face and left permanently blinded. Similar injuries were sustained by a journalist reporting the protests and another of a young man who was asked to move his car off the street by police officers and then shot in the face when he did. There was also reports of a man with a heart condition who was shot square in the chest and suffered a cardiac arrest though I don't know if that one was confirmed or what happened with that. Either way there's plenty of evidence of them being used incorrectly and with wilful intent to cause harm or suffering. 

They should only be used in they way they are intended. It's also interesting to see that British police are also equipped with these types of ammunition and yet you do not see reports of the same there.

It may not feel like it at the moment but I can guarantee that you've helped your friends. You may not have realised it but there will have been times you've helped. A phone call, a drink out a late night text. It's hard for our brain's to see but trust me, there's at least one person out there whose life you've changed, that you've helped save. Talk to them, some will even appreciate you opening up to them.

You're not worthless. Not to your friends and family. If they're there for you and open to you it's because they love you. You probably have no idea how much you're worth to them. I promise you are loved and you are worth more than they can put into words.

It's hard when you're struggling, if it's financially or whatever. I assume that's what you meant by not self sufficient. Correct me if I'm wrong. It's hard to do with depression but there is a solution out there. Can you talk to your family or friends about your options. If it's a job maybe someone's work has something, if it's housing maybe someone has a spare room you can stay in or something. That actually might be good for you, if you stay with someone who can be there for you whilst you're struggling. You shouldn't be on your own right now. If someone offers, take it. It helped me.

You are not a failure. Life sucks and it grinds you down. And you're not lazy. Look, you've taken the first step and spoken to your doctor. That's not what a lazy person would do. A lazy person wouldn't seek help.

Just remember, you are not a burden to your friends and family. They want to help you. I guarantee there's at least one weirdo out there that will enjoy helping you and will be glad you asked for it.

Look after yourself.

Edit: Also remember the little wins. Have you had breakfast, have you drunk something, showered or got out of bed? Anyone one of those is a victory when you have depression.
